\[
c_i = \operatorname{DWT}_{1D}\big(p_{\theta_i}\big),
\quad
T_i = k\, \hat{\sigma}_i,
\quad
\hat{\sigma}_i = \frac{\operatorname{median}(|d_{1,i}|)}{0.6745},
\qquad
\hat{I} = \operatorname{FBP}\Big(\operatorname{IDWT}_{1D}\big(\eta_{T_i}(c_i)\big)\Big),
\qquad
n = 180,\ J = 4,\ k = 3
\]

The formula shows the default parameter values.

where

- \(p_{\theta_i}\): The projection at angle theta_i
- \(c_i\): The ridgelet coefficients of projection i, its 1-D wavelet coefficients
- \(d_{1,i}\): The finest details of projection i
- \(k\): The threshold factor
- \(\eta_T\): The shrink rule with threshold T
- \(J\): The number of levels of the 1-D transform

A ridgelet is constant along lines in one direction and a wavelet across them. Candes and Donoho showed that the ridgelet transform is a 1-D wavelet transform applied along the projections of the Radon transform. A straight line in the image is a single point in the sinogram, so it gives a few large ridgelet coefficients, while noise spreads over many small ones. Here p_theta_i are the projections of the radon-filter entry, c_i their 1-D wavelet coefficients and d_1,i the finest details of projection i. The noise level of each projection is estimated from d_1,i, and the threshold T_i is k times that level. eta is the shrink rule of wavelet thresholding. FBP is filtered back projection with the ramp filter. The sampled Radon transform and FBP are not exact inverses, so this is an approximation. Do and Vetterli built an exactly invertible finite ridgelet transform, which needs a prime image size.
